SHIP-RAISING IN SEVASTOPOL. Correspondcuci' of ttio N. V. Tribune Sevastopol, Sept. 1, 1858. la tny last I stated that we had raised the following vessels sunk at the head of South Bay, viz: Empress Cathrine, 120 guns; Chesina, 84 guns; frigate , 60 guns ; a small vessel, name not known. These were blown to pieces and of course raised in fragments. The þÿCompany s \ share of the materials was probably 100,000 rubles; exponses, however, to be deducted We have now lying at our wharf the gun-brig Semelai, or Bold, which we raised entire. Next was the beautiful steamer Turk, captured from the Turks during the commencement of the war. She was built expiessly for the Sultan, and used as a yacht. Her engines were comparatively in j perfect order, her hull but little injured, ana ;..>t at all worm-eaten. The Russian Government appraised her her cepted at a at 60,000 rubles, $45,000, ,ul trifle under the valuation. The next was the Goisnoi, a war-steamer which was built in 1838, and is of course quite old, but nevertheless perfectly sound, uninjured by worms, her engines in good condition, with massive copper boilers, and cost in England wheu new, £15,000. The Government has not decided to accept her ; if broken, the materials will be worth probably $40,000. We have four steamers slung aud ready to raise, and we have had some difficulty with the war-steamer Danube, to which our caissons are now fastened. She is of iron, and so heavy that the forward chain cut her completely in two, which a very is serious matter, as

she cannot be pumped dry when raised to the surface; but in my next, I hope to give you a detailed account of her, with four others. Our i oaissons work admirably, but had they been of double their capacity, the power derived from them would bo immense. Wc shall immediately construct two others of large dimensions, and although wo have been hero fifteen months, all

can never be recovered, unless some Yankee will invent a wind-mill pump of sufficient power to empty the Black Sea. If coffer dams were built across the entrance to the Bosphorus, Sea of Azof, and the various rivers that empty into these basins, all the treasure found in Sebastopol Harbor alone would cancel the cost. As you are given at home to magnificent enterprises, to Pacific Railroads, canals across the Isthmus of Panama, tremendous tunnels, and Atlantic Telegraph Cables, 1 shall expect to see in some future number of The Scientific American a diagram of such a pump. The only requisite is that it should empty the Black Sea, and carry off the water. But to return : We have three Greek parties employed, numbering about 150 men. They dive without armor, and are quite successful, receiving as a compensation a fourth part of what they raise. A short time since, one of them brought up ft piece of iron four feet long, with 35 gold imperials firmly imbedded in the oxyd formed upon the bolt. The declarations of the President in regard to his foreign policy, are plain and unmistakeable, and are in perfect accordance with the famous Ostend Manifesto. After the purchase of Cuba has been effected, we suppose we shall hear of þÿ the imperative and overruling law of self-preþÿservation demanding the acquisition of other islands and territories. THE PACIFIC RAILROAD. i would again call your attention to the construction of a Pacific railroad. Time and reflection have but served to confirm me in the trutli and justice of the observations which I made on this subject in my last annual message, to which I beg leave respectfully to refer. It is freely admitted that it would be inexpedient for this government to exercise the power of constructing the Pacific railroad by its own immediate agents. Such a policy would increase the patronage of the executive to' a dangerous extent, and introduce a system of jobbing and corruption which no vigilance on the part of fed <ral officials could either prevent or detect. This can only bo done by the keen eye, and active and careful supervision, of individual ami private interest. The cons: ruction of this road ought, therefore, to be committed to companies incorporated by the States, or other agencies whose pecuniary interests would he directly involved. Congress might then assist them in tlio work by grants of land or of money, or both, under such conditions and restrictions as would secure the transportation of troops and munitions ot war free from any charge, and that of the United Stetes mail at a fair and reasonable price. The progress of events since the commencement of our last session has shown how soon difficulties disr before a firm and determined resolution. At tip such a road was deemed by wise and patrimen to be a visionary project. The great distance overcome, and the intervening mountains and

d' erts in the way, were obstacles which, in the opinion of many, could not be surmounted. Now, after the lapse of but a single year, these obstacles, it has been discovered, are far less formidable than they were supposed to be ; and mail stages, with passengers, now pass and repass regularly twice in cacii week, by a common wagon road between San Francisco and St. Louis and Memphis, in less than twenty five days. The service Ins been as regularly performed as it was in former years between New York and this city. Whilst disclaiming all authority to appropriate money for the construction of this road, except that derived from the war making power of the constitution, there are important collateral considerations urging us to undertake the work as speedily as possible. The first and most momentous of these is, that such a road would be a powerful bond of union between the States east and west of the Rocky Mountains. This is so self-evident as to require no illustration. But again, iu a commercial point of view I consider this the great quest on of the day. With the eastern front of our republic stretching along the Atlantic, and its western front along the Pacific, if all the parts should be united by a safe, easy, and rapid intercommunication, wo must necessarily command a very large proportion of the trade both of Europe and Asia. Our recent treaties with China and Japan will open these rich and populous empires to our commerce : and the history of the world proves that the nation which

lias gained possession of the trade with Eastern Asia has always become woalt v an I powerful. The peculiar geographical position ol California and our Pacific possessions invites Ann .is-an capital and enterprise into this fruitful field. To reap the rich harvest, however, it is an indispensable prc-requisitc that we shall first have a railroad, to convey and circulate its products throughout every portion of the Union. Besides, such a railroad through our temperate latitude, which would not be impelled by the frosts and snows of winter, nor by the tropical heats of summer, would attract to itself much of the travel and the trace of all nations passing between Europe and Asia

n m i. From Haiti and Jamaica we have the anticipated news of the fall of the Empire of Haiti, and of the Emperor and family in exile. A perusal of the particulars, here subjoined, will shew that niter General Geffrard, the Emperor owes his existence to the fortunate circumstance of a vessel from Port-au-Prince the British transport ship Melbourne, with spoken having troops, bound to England, and to the Commander Laving resolved to go to that port in order to render such assistance as may have been needed by the Europeans residing in tbe island, should it unfortunately have proved a war of caste. This, we are happy to say, was not so, and that Capt. MeCrca was as ready to afford succour to the Chief of the State as he would have been to 1 the Europeans had the case been otherwise. We furnish an extract from a private letter, I under date of 21st Jauuaiy, which gives pro- ! mise of great prosperity to the country in the future : þÿ þÿ You will have been informed by the last mail of the then unsatisfactory position of the country-4-politically anil commercially þÿ and wo are now giad to inform you that the þÿ black cloud on tbe þÿhorizon lias bceu almost, if not altogether, dissipated, and a brighter future is not now, we think, far distant. The abolition of the Empire, and the re-establishment of a Republic, was proclaimed here on Tuesday evening betweeu 6 and 7 o'clock. This has been the most bloodless revolution that has ever taken place in Hayti; we believe there has only been

one man killed, and that more by accident than intention. This is som thing new in the annals of Hayti, particularly as it happens to be the downfall of a Black Government, and the reinstalment of a Colored one. From St. Marcs the Emperor made a precipitate retreat to the capital, which lie entered on the 11th General Geffrard followed him by easy marehos and arrived towards the evening of the 14th. During the night the Imperial troops and the insurgents began to þÿ þÿFraternize, and at 4 þÿo clockin the morning the þÿKmporor spalace was surrounded and we are told that it required the united efforts of Geffrard and Lis Generals to protect the. Emperor from the exasperated multitude. He was however safely conveyed from the Palace to the French Consulate, aud cm barked on board a British transport in tbe afternoon in destination lor Jamaica after having signed his abdication. There areteveral decrees and documents from the new Government in town, but as they arc yet in the Press wo have not seen any of them. Phe abolition of the Empire has given universal satisfaction. The country has had a ten years trial of botilouquc, and the people arc only too glad to get quit of him, even at a sacrifice of their constitutional animosities. However, unless the present ruler displays as much tact in diplomacy as ho has shewn capacity as a General, we run a great chance of seeing the country again embroiled in a civil war. Wo sincerely hope, however, that be will be judicious in

bis selection of parties to tlio respective places ol honor and profit, in which case every thing will go on well. It seems the inhabitants gcm rally cannot yet exactly realise the idea of their comparative freedom : the country people do not coroe to town, and the Marchandes are still afraid to buy ; but we doubt not this feeling of timidity will soon disappear, and a brisk trade þÿfollow. The Jamaica ,l Colonial þÿStandard, of tbe 25th January, gives the following succinct account of the Emperor's arrival at Kingston: þÿ The presence of the late Emperor of Haiti in this city, as au applicant for the protection of our Government and our laws, marks another era in the history of that noble but unfortunate country. It is not our purpose at the present moment to enter into a criticism of the political circumstances which have consigned this rather remarkable personage ns a refugee to our shores. Wo derirc at, present simply to lay before our readers a full and succinct detail of the actual events attending tire þÿEmperor s abdication, gathered from tbe most unexceptionable sources, and in doing so rse teel it our duty to express our warm gratification þÿ a gratification which we arc sure will be gem rously participated in and reflected by Her M þÿty Government s þÿ at the happy accident which enabled Captain McCrc, R. A., who chanced to bo in command of a considerable number of H. M. troops on board the

troop ship Melbourne, on the route to England, to afford the substantial aid by which alone, under Providence, the lives of the exiled Sovereign, his family, and Ministry, have been preserved. It appears that on the 10th January the Emperor re-entered Port-un- Prince ; having fought several partial engagements with the iusurgeut General, Gcffrard, in all of which he had been worsted by the desertion of his troops to the enemy. lie immediately commenced barricading the city, and throwing up earthworks on commanding points. On the following day alarm guns were hied to announce to the people that the insurgent army was in sight. The greatest anarchy and confusion were the immediate consequence, increased by reports of the approach of the lawless mountain peasantry, and. worse than all, that the Emperor had been advised to mak hc revolution an affair of caste, and, by sacrificing the whole of the white and coloured people, secure the pure negro interest in his own behalf. It is generally believed that horrors, of which the former history of that city affords terrible examples, would have been perpetrated, had not the wise discretion of the British Consul- General detained the Melbourne transport in the harbour; on board which vessel, brought into within a mile of the landing place from the usual anchorage, Captain McCrea, the officer in command of the troops, had them ready, day and night, to afford instant assistance to the European residents. Genoral Gcffrard, however, instead of storm-

ing the city, determined to undermine the Emþÿperor authority s by his agents, and lay outside the walls until the 14th January, during which titno numbers of the þÿEmperor s troops passed over to the insurgent army, until, all being ripe, on the morning of the 15th, at 3 a m., General Geffrard burst into the city; the forts were instantly escaladed and taken without loss, and the þÿEmperor Palace s surrounded. The Emperor immediately despatched a deputation to General Gcffrard, demanding his protection as far as the French Consulate, which was grauted ; and where the Emperor aud Empress, with their family and baggage, arrived in safely, escorted by 300 of his Guards, who still remained faithful, but who immediately after disbanded. The Emperor at once assembled the officers of State, and by their advice signed his abdication, which, together with the renaissance of the Republic, was proclaim, d by sound of trumpet through the city. Meanwhile, early on the morning of the 15th, three of the Ministers of the cx-Einperor, who bad made themselves þÿunpopular namely, Genoral Vil de Gubin, governor of Port-au-Prince, General þÿD Elva, Grand Chancellor of the Empire, and formerly Minister to the Court of St. James, and General l)e- salines, Chiif of the Police þÿ succeeded in gaining the refuge of the Consulate, which, surrounded by a mob of thousands yelling for their blood, and crowded with the relations of these refugees, presented the appearance of a Babel. The French Consul immediately communicated

his embarrassing position to the Republican Government, and the result was an order for the ex-Emperor to quit Haity, as best he might, immediately, with a prnmiso that he should have a body of t roops to piotect hint, i f possible , as far us the wharf. The Emperor having decided on going to Jamaica, and as his life would not have been safe for a moment on board a Merchant ship, the French Charge d' Affaires, M. Mallmet, called upon Mr. Byron, the. British Consul General, for permission to embark him on board the Melbourne. Leave was iustantly given, aud notice sent to Captain McCrea, the officer in command of II. M. Troops on board that vessel to make preparations to receive him. These being effected, Captain McCrea reported himself ready at. the French Consulate at 4 p- m., when it was determined to attempt the embarkation through the dense masses of people who had collected in the streets. Supported by Capt. McCrea on one side, by the French Charge on the other, with the Imperial family following close, and surrounded by the European Cousuls aud English officers, the cortege of Exiles issued from the door of the Consulate, þÿ amid yells, and groans, and shouts of Vive la Rtpublique þÿ/ Many in the crowd were armed with pistols, swords and stones ; but none dared attempt anything while the Exiles

® ®® l«l S', were thus encompassed by men generally respected even by a Canaille thirsting for revenge. lu this manner, foot by foot was gained along t' e streets leading tv ie wharf, through vust crowds of the yelling and highly excited populace, which, on the quay before the boats, made a final push to break through the escort without success, but was, with great difficulty, restrained from pushing the whole party into the Sea. Lying off, about 20 yards, were two guard bouts filled with English Artillerymen, who clos d on the boats containing the Imperial Exiles, aud sheltered them until the protection of the Merchant Shipping was gained, and the yells aud execrations of disappointed thousands were shut out from the ears of the exiled party. The Canaille, thus foiled, instantly returned to the Consolate, which they once more surrounded in the hope of preventing the escape of the three Ministers who were obnoxious to the people. For three days and nights they guarded iu all directions every door and possible means of escape, during which their cries aud groans wore incessant. At length, on the night of the 17 1 h January, a large fire broke out in the city, aud the idea at once ran among the mob to fire the Consulate, aud so compel the refugees to come forth. Hearing this, the French Charge utterly exhausted and worn out, with the full consent of the English 'Consul General, sent off a boat to the Met. bourse, requesting Capt. McCrea to come to Ins immediate assistance. In half an hour 150 men of II. M. Artil-

lery had landed, and, marching in perfect order and silence up two different streets., closed round the Consulate, and separated the crowd from it. In an instant the savage yells that had previously predominated, gave way to doubt, fear, and wonder. In less than an hour, the Ministers of the new Government, having been informed of the landing of the English troops, galloped down from the lhtlace in full uniform, escorted by troops; when on questionin': the officer in command of the British troops, and receiving his explanation, the Minister replied that, under the extraordinary circumstances in which the country was placed, he, the British officer, had acted with perfect correctness, and gave him, in the name of the President, his warmest thanks. A conference was at once held in tiio office of the Consolate, the result of which was that the Republic accepted the responsibility of guarding the Consulate, and promised that a large body of troops should be despatched at once ; and, further, that a proclamation should lio issued, warning the people no longer to surround þÿ thehouse. The Charge þÿd affaires of France, therefore, as soon as he was able, dismissed, with thanks, the English troops, who re-embarked in perfect silence and order on board the Melbourne, having greatly astonished the population of Port-au- Prince by the order and discipline observed by them in the ranks when on duty. I Tiie two following nights, by the admirable arrangements made by the French charge, the Ministers

K21HE undersigned begs leave to acquaint Sx the public, that she has taken over the dealing of her late husband Anthony Phe/an, by Government's grant. She begs further to state, that the mercantile business will be carried on by her at the same place in Company Street, near the Weekday Market, and trusts that she will receive liberal patronage. Those persons, who have kindly dealt with her late husband and whose accounts are yet unpaid, are politely solicited to come forward with payment, to enable her to liquidate the debts against the establishment. She offers for sale A double-seat Phaeton with double harness, either separately or together : And for rent House No. 29 Market Street, this town, on moderate terms. Christiansted, 3d March 1859. LOUISA PHELAN.

We have received a copy of tho New York Church Journal of the 2titk January, containing an accouut, written in this Island, of the visit of the Bishop of Antigua iu December last year. We have been requested to copy the article, which coutains in the response of the Bishop to a few remarks made by the ltector Dr. Hawley, at an entertainment held at the Ilectory, some remarks complimentary to the Danish Nation ; but we must respectfully decline doing so. It was held in the restored gallery of the Palace of tho Louvre called the Salle des Etats, which is on the first storey of the transverse building separating tho two courts, and which is destined for the reception ui the great bodies of the State. When completed it will communicate with the picture gallery. The hall is an oblong, 42 metres long, 21 wide, and 16 high. It is fine in its proportions, hut seems hardly spacious enough lor such a ceremony as the present. At the farther end is raised an cstradc of six steps, on which the throne stands, under a canopy of rich crimson velvet, gorgeously embroidered, with richly gilt pillars on each side displaying the Imperial arms, and surmounted by the crown and the Imperial eagle. Rows of benches covered with crimson velvet stand in Iront to the right and left, and gradually descend to the flour, which is richly carpeted. To the right of the throne, on a levol with tho platform, and under the gallery which, supported on gilt columns, runs round tho interior of the hall, a tribune was set apart for tho Empress, the Princess Clotilda, and their respective ladies in waiting. A little before 1 tho Empress aud the Princess Clotildu entered, and were conducted by the Grand Master of the Ceremonies to their places in the tribune close was saluted with the cry of " Vive I'lmpcratrice !" to and to tho right of the throne. His Majesty, who, as usual, wore the uniform of a general officer, with the star and riband of the Legion of Honour, stood up, and, amid deep aud apparently anxious silence, read, iu a distinct manner, the following speech from the throne : þÿ " Messieurs les Secateurs þÿ Messieurs les 1) puties " France has, as you are aware, during tho þÿ last six years, seen her welfare augmented, !,er riches increase, her internal dissensions die out, her influence restored, aud yet there arises ut intervals in the midst of the general calm and prosperity a vague anxiety, a hollow agitation, which, without any well-defined cause, possesses itself of Certain minds and shakes public confidence. I deplore these periodical discouragements without being astonished at them. In a society shattered like ours by so many revolutions time alono can confirm convictions, give renewed vigour to character and create a political faith. The auxiety which has just been produced, without the appearance of imminent dangers, may justly cause surprise, for it gives evidence, at the same time, of too much distrust and of

too much alarm. A doubt seems to have arisen, on the one baud, of tho moderation of which 1 have given so many proof's, and, on the other, of the power of France. Happily, the great mass of the people is far from sharing such impressions as these. To-day it is my duty again to explain to you afresh what it seems to have forgotten. " What has been constantly my policy ? To reassure Europe, and to restore to France her real rank, to cement strictly our alliance with England, and arrange with tho Continental Bowers of Europe the degree of my friendship, aceoiding to the similarity of our views, and to the nature of their proceedings as regards France. It was thus that ou the eve of my third election I made at Bordeaux the declaration, ' I, 'Empire e'est la paix ;' wishing thereby to prove that if the heir of the Emperor Napoleon reascended the thron" he would not renew un era of conquests, but would inaugurate a system of peace which could not be disturbed, except for the defence of great national interests. " As to the alliance of France and England, I have employed all my perseverance to consolidate it, aud I have found ou the other side of the Channel a fortunate icciprocity of sentiments on tho part of the Queen of Great Britain, as well as on the part of statesmen of all opinions. To attaiu the same end, so useful to the peace of the world, I have on every oecasiou trampled under loot the irritating remembrances of tho past, the attacks of calumny, aud even the national prejudices of my country. This alliance

has home its fruits; not only have we acquired together a lasting glory in the East, but again at the extremity of the world we have just thrown open an immense empire to the progress ol civilisation and of the Christian religion. "Since tho conclusion of peace, my relations with the Emperor of Russia have assumed the character of the most frank cordiality, because we have been in accord ou all points under dispute. THE PROSPECTS OF WAR. The Paris correspondent of the Times writes on Thursday: þÿ "As to whether peace or war shall prevail there is still a diversity of opinion, and though I do not subscribe to all he says, yet I caunot but repeat the opinion of a person who is entitled to respect, and who possesses much experience in political life. He is not inclined to think that the present difficulties urc such as are likely to be resolved by diplomacy. He thinks war inevitable ; but that the date depends on circumstances (this I must admit to be a safe margin); but he believes that, before the year is out, hostilities will commence. As for the negotiations which Austria would consent to open, ho thinks that she may do so to gain time, either for military preparations, or to secure the alliances of which she stands in need. In any case, the said negotiations can only have reference to the evacuation of the Roman States by the Austrian and French troops. This evacuation, ho says, is precisely what would suit the Emperor of the French, whose plans would be promoted by an insurrection in Italy. Now, so long as his troops are at Rome the Emperor would be obliged to put down a seditious movement on one point which he would see with secret pleasure break out in Lombardy. Austria has motives of quite a contrary kind to remain in the Roman States To quit them would be to fall blindly into a snare. She will, perhaps, appear to lend herself to negotiations on this point, but, as I have already said, only to gain
time.''

Mr. Editor, As one of the Community who feels a deep interest in the subject at present under discussion in the þÿ þÿAvis regarding the stipends which have been so long withheld from the English and Roman Catholic Congregations, I can not rofrain front offering my sincere, though feeble, thanks to þÿ a Member of the Colonial þÿCouncil for the opportunity he is thus giving an anxious public, to fairly judge for themselves

regarding this long þÿ vexed þÿquestion, by layiug before them a clear and simple narrative of facts ; and to you also, Sir, the public thanks are due, for your impartial and able advocacy of the matter in hand. This valuable and instructive exposition of the case carries with it, in some of its details, a sad evidence of how hard it is to wring even-handed justice from the grasp of prejudiced or unwilling minds. Amdocs it appear, I must admit, that the fault lies with the high r authority, which seems willing enough that the aids sought for should be granted. The course adopted in bringing this matter before the public iu all its lengthy details, and in a connected form, so that it may be understood, becomes the more necessary, as the public can gain little information from the meagre and tasdy reports which emanate from the Burgher Council regarding their proceedings ; for, even in that body, I understand, things are not particularly well regulated so as to ensure the members a fair and uninterrupted hearing at all times, upon such questions as come before the board for debate. 1 can not of course speak from my own particular knowledge, for although a representative body, the public are shut out from its deliberations. But if I have not had an opportunity of being present at any of their sittings as one of their constituents, I have had opportunities of witnessing the proceedings ns carried on in public representative bodies in other Countries where,

among other things, 1 have always observed that when a question was once declared opeu tin- debate, the person occupying the chair, after delivering his own sentiments, if bethought proper, secured to the members in succession, if they desired, a proper hearing ; calmly listening himself to the arguments of each until all were hc.nd who wished to address the chair. That functionary in no case, that I noticed, scented to consider that it was a part of his duly, during the discussions which arose upon any question before the assembly þÿ to keep up a sort of contest or running tire with each por- -<>n whose opinion lie might differ from, and mb avour the while to urge his own views of the question, so as to make it necessary often for the person addressing the chair, to claim his privilege of having the þÿ þÿword. If the chairman, or speaker, of the House of Commons in England, or the House of Representatives in Washington, had to do the principal part of the talking, in either of these bodies, in order to carry the house with him in his endeavours to eliiuin.ve the opinions of members and enforce I is own upon the various questions brought forward, a numerous relay of tln-se functionaries would he required in such case. Before concluding these desultory remarks, l feel induced to observe that the result of the last Burgher Council election in Christiansted, is worthy to be noted as furnishing a significant illustration of what the Community can do when sufficiently interested in any question

important enough to induce them to concentrate their votes þÿ the selected candidate having re eeived 57 votes, against 1 7 thrown for the one supposed not favorable to the granting of the aid to the Churches. Your obedient servant. One of the 57 voters.

The article in your þÿ Avis of 11th inst., regarding the estates, which had none, or very few labourers at work on the 27th þÿDec , r and 3rd January, is quite to the purpose, and very correct in observation : but, there are. other evils, to one of which I take leave to call the attention, of those agents and managers, who have a desire to do their duty faithfully. It is the very shameful manner, or perhaps 1 should rather say time, that the labourers turn out to work, upon many estates ; both in the mornings and afternoons. On a great many estates, ! the people þÿdon turn t out, even in the longest days, until half past seven in þÿ half past two in the afternoon some even later. the morning, and This is one hour jtr. day lost, five pr. week, and amounts to the full figure of 26 working days pr. year. Let me ask these Gentlemen who in the face of the law, allow such an extravagant j waste of time, to pause and scrutinize my calculations. Are they correct gentlemen? If they : are, then why hire labor of a Saturday, before you have fully tried what you have at your , disposal during the weok ? Here Mr. Editor

? O' ft 0 ft ft v \1 is a serious loss to every interest of the country j as also Ilis þÿMajesty s revenue. No one i certainly, will have the assurance to deny, that i agriculture, and agriculture only, is the life of all and every establishment lieu ; therefore) it should be the primary consideration, with every I reflecting man in the community, to promote its interests, thereby assisting their own, but Alas ! Alas ! ! The Government, or police are not iu the slightest degree to blame for the evil I have pointed out : notwithstanding this belief, I am fully of opinion it never will be remedied without tlieir aid. s Our labourers are, most of them, good people, and require good precedent to act as faithfully as many others ; but, if they see a want of industry aud careless habits, in those who should set them an example, are they so much to blame, to follow the fashion ? CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. FRIDAY, 11th MARCH, IS69. Intercolonial Intelligence. | From Jamaica we learn that a very gravo resistance to the law, on the part of the labouring classes, took place during the last week in February. Every turnpike gate in the Parish of Westmoreland, with the toll houses attached to j them, were pulled down aud destroyed. It is said that upwards of five thousand of the people, of both sexes, were engaged in these outrages. þÿ To make the matter þÿworse says the Colonial Standard, þÿ threats were held out that if any magistrate in the parish interfered to bring any of the parties criminally concerned to justice, his property would he set fire þÿto. The cause of these outrages appeals to be some opposition, on the part of these classes, to the tax upon horses, mules and asses, which is the only direct tax tiiat in any way affects them. Immigration appears to be extensively kept up in Trinidad. Twelve ships have been chartered for the season, and seven had already arrived from Madras and Calcutta. THE þÿQUEEN S SPEECH, My Lords and Gentlemen, In recurring, at the usual season, to the advice of my Parliament, I am happy to think that in the internal state of the country there is nothing to excite disquietude, and much to call tor satisfaction and thankfulness. Pauperism and crime have considerably diminished during the past year, and a spirit of general contentment prevails. The blessing of the Almighty on the valour of my troops in India, and on the skill of their commanders, lias enabled me to inflict signal chastisement upon those who are still iu arms against my authority, whenever they have ventured to encounter my forces ; and I trust that, at no distant period, I may be able to announce to you the complete pacification of that great Empire, and to devote my attention to the improvement of its condition, and to the obliteration of all traces of the present unhappy conflict. On assuming, by your advice, the direct government of that portion of my dominions, I deemed it proper to

make known by proclaumt on the principles by which it was my intention to be guided, and the clemency which f was disposed to show towards those who might have been seduced into revolt, but who might be willing to return to tlieir allegiance. 1 have directed that a copy of that proclamation should be laid before you. I receive from all Foreign Powers assurances of their li ndly feelings. To cultivate and confirm those i feelings, to maintain inviolate the faith of public treaties, and to contribute, as far as my influence can extend, to the preservation of the general peace, are the objects of iuj unceasing solicitude. 1 have concluded, with the Sovereigns who were parlies to the Treaty of Paris of lbiti. a Convention relative to the organisation of the Prncipalities of Moldavia and Wallaclna. These Rouman Provinces are now proceeding lo establish, under its provisions, tlieir new form of government. A treaty of commerce which I have concluded with the Emperor of Russia, and which will be laid before you, is a satisfactory indication of tlie complete reestablishment of those amicable relations which, until tlieir late unfortunate interruption, hail long subsisted between us, to the mutual advantage of our respective dominions. The measures which, in consort with my ally the Emperor of the French, I thought it necessary to take upon the coast of China have resulted in a treaty, by which further (Fusion of blood lias been prevented, and which holds out the prospect of greatly increased

intercourse with that extensive and densely-peopled empire. Another treaty into which I have entered with the Emperor of Japan opens a fresh field for commercial enterprise in a populous and highly-civilised country which has hitherto been jealously guarded against the intrusion of foreigners. As soon as the ratifications of these treaties shall have been exchanged they will be laid before you. . I have great satisfaction in announcing to you that the Emperor of the French has abolished a system of negro emigration from the east coast of Africa, against which, as unavoidably tending, however guarded, to the encouragement of the slave trade, my Government has never ceased to address to Ins Imperial Majesty its most earnest hut friendly representations. This wise act on the part of liis Imperial Majesty induces me to hope that negotiations now in progress at þÿl aris may tend to the total abandonment of llie system, and to tlie substitution of a duly regulated supply of substantially free labour. The state of the Republic of Mexico, distracted by civil war, has induced me to carry forbearance to its utmost limits in regard to wrongs a id indignities to which British residents have been subjected at the hands of the two contending parties. They have at length been carried to such an extent that I have been compelled to give instructions to the Commander of my Naval Forces in those seas to demaud, and if necessary to enforce, due reparation. Gentlemen ot the House of Commons, I have directed that the Estimates lor the ensuing

year shall be submitted to you. They have been framed with a due regard to economy, and to the efficiency of the public service. The universal introduction of steam power into naval warfare will render necessary a temporary increase of expenditure in providing for the reconstruction of tiie 13r.ti-h Navy ; but 1 am persuad d that you will cheerfully vote whatever sums you may find to be requisite for an object of such vital importance as the maintenance of the maritime power of the country. My Lords and Gentlemen, Your labours have, i,. recent Sessions, been usefully directed to various measures of legal and social improvement. In tee belief that further measures of a similar charactei may bo wisely and beneficially introduccd, I have desired that lulls may be submitted to you without delay for assimilating and amending the laws relating to bankruptcy and insolvency ; for bringing logo her into one set of statutes, in a classified form and with such modifications as experience will suggest to you, the aws relating to crimes and offences in England mil Ireland ; for enabling the owners of land in England to obtain for themselves an indefeasible title to their estati and interests, aud lor registering such titles witii simplicity and security. Your attenlh i will lie call d to the state of the laws which regulate the representation of the people in Parliament, and I cannot d .lit but that you will give to this great subject it degr of calm and impartial consideration proportioned to the magnitude of the

interests involved iu the result of your discussions. These, and other propositions for the amendment of the laws, whicn will be brought under your notice as the progress of public bus ness may permit, I commend to the exercise ol your deliberate judgment ; and earnestly pray that your counsels may be so guided as to insure the stability of the Throne, the maintenance aud improvement ot our institutions, and tlie general wellare and happiness of my people. The Monxtcur of Saturday morning contains an article of which the following is an extract : þÿ The serious condition of Italian affairs has attracted the attention of the Emperor, whose endeavours are to conclude alliances in furtherance of the interest of France. The Emperor has promised the King of Sardinia to protect him against any aggressive act of Austria, but his promis s extend no further. The Emperor denies that France is now making warlike preparations : she has not exceeded the effective force she is accustomed to have during peace. Assuming that preparations in the aiseuals have received any extraordinary impulse, it is only because changes were necessary in our materiel, our artillery, and in the whole of our fleet. All our naval preparations arc limited to the arming of four frigates and four transports, to meet different emergencies. It is quite absurd to represent the Emperor as pushing on war, and to cast on hint alone the responsibility of having amused uneasiness, aud of having caused warlike preparations in Europe. Where can any one point out words, diplomatic notes, or acts implying the wish of the Emperor to provoke war '! The Emperor is now txuminii.g the various reasons of the present complications, but tiiis must not be regarded as any provocation of war on his part. Besides, to examine these questions is to meet them in a diplomatic way, and nothing authorises the belief that the issue will not be favourable to the consolidation of peace.

The Bombay correspondent of the Daily News writes : þÿ The rebellion in Oude has been brought to a brilliant close. Peace is re-established, and tranquility and order prevail where anarchy and confusion so lately reigned. In my last,! mentioned that the principal rebel leaders had been driven across the Raptee into Nepaul ; that their followers were dispirited and disorganised, and that they were without provisions or supplies of any kind. Since then their position has not improved. The combined armies of the Begum, the Nana and Beni Madhoo, amount to about 12,000 men of all arms. They occupy position a across the Nepaul frontier, not very far from Bankee, the scene of their last defeat. It was at first supposed that Jung Behadoor would not assume any prompt offensive attitude with regard to the fugitives. But he has agreeably deceived public expectation by at once taking up a decisive position. He no sooner heard that they had croi-sed tbo Raptee and entered his territories than he issued a proclamation to the effect that all murderers and rebels in arms

The Ghoorka army was at once moved downward, in the direction of the rebel position, and an application forwarded to Lord Clyde for troops to co-operate with the army of Nepaul Brigadier Horsford was ordered upon this duty, and his brigade has already crossed the llaptee to join the Ghoorka army By the time the next mad leaves, I shall, in all likelihood, have intelligence of a battle to communicate, as the British and Nepaulese Geiieials wil,, doubtless, bring matters at once to an issue. A number of regiments have been ordered home, amongst which are the 9 h Lancers and Maude's bat ery. Arrival of the Neapolitan Exiles in Ireland. The following interesting particulars connected with the arrival in Queenstowo of the American vessel having on board the Neapolitan exiles, are supplied by the Cork Examiner of Monday night ; þÿ Great sensation was created in Queenstown yesterday morning by the arrival of the American ship David Stewart, ol Baltimore, Captain Prentiss, 674 tons register, having on board the celebrated Poerio aud bis companions, whom the recent act of grace of the Neapolitan Government had set free from the duugeons of that State. It will be remembered that, though pardoned, they were sentenced to banishment, and that, after having been deported from their native country to Spain, it was afterwards determined that they should be sent to America. Accordingly, the David Stewart was chartered to take them from Cadiz to New York, where upon landing each was to receive a sum of 120 dollars, and be released from all further control. They had been brought from Naples to Cadiz in a Neapolitan transport, from which, after about three weeks, they were put on board the David Stewart. On the 19th of February they were placed on board the ves-el destined for them, where tbey received accommodation of the best kind possible The Dayid Stewart is a large new American ship, and was able to give first-class accommodation to 44 of the party ; the remainder were allocated second-class berths, but were placed on equal terms in every other respect. All the party having been put on

board, the David Stewart was towed out to sea for a distance of nearly 200 miles by the Stromboli, Neapolitan war steamer, so as to give her a good offing. The steamer then cast off, and left the ship with a fair wind from the east. Scarcely, however, was the ship well away from the protection of the steamer's guus than the exiles in a body came to the captain, delivered to bim a protest against being carried to New York, and called upon bim to make for the first port be conld reach in England. The captain,

one-third of whose freight bad been retained as a guarantee for the performance of his contract, remonstrated with them upon tbeir demand to have hitn break bis engagement, and ultimately refused. They appeared to acquiesce in bis decision, or at least pressed tbeir demand no further that evening ; but the next morning it was again renewed, aud in a more decided and threatening manner. This part of the transaction brought out au incident which had a touch of romance in it. A young Italian, named Raffaelle Settembrini, had shipped with the captain in Cadix, and signed articles as a seaman. Up to that morning he had done his work with the rest of the crew. But when the assemblage waited upou the captain he made his appearance in the uniform of a mate of one of the Galway line of steamers þÿ a handsome blue frock, with gilt buttons, gold cap-band, &c. This position he really had held, and we caunot say whether or not he does still. But it turned out that he was the son of one of the most prominent of the exiles. Luigi Setti mbrini, who, hearing of his father's conditional pardon, aud of his destination, left for Spain, aud resorted to the ruse we have mentioned to join him The captain of the ship is of opinion that there wag an even more important object in his so acting than merely to enjoy the society of his father. He believes that he was dispatched by the Italian Society in London to aid the prisoners in the course they subsequently took. However that may be, certain it is that his presenee made

the exiles more confident in their demand. They stated that they had a navigator in their party, aud that, even if they bad to take the ship out of the bands of the captain and crew, they would be able to sail her without tbeir assistance. They represented to the captain that they had been two months at sea, many of them being old, and all with constitutions more or less enfeebled by an imprisonment of 10 years, so that a loug voyage would be torture to all of them, and death perhaps to some. Tbey contended also that being under the American flag they were free, and that he had no right to take them anywhere but where they ehose. These arguments, backed up by the preponderance of physical foroe, the exiles being 66, while the crew were but 17, and the manifest determination of the former to resort to extremities to carry out their intention, compelled the captain to yield, and turn the vessel's head northward. They were, indeed, temperate and polite in manner, but about tbeir determination there could be no mistake. In fact his resolute passengers were not satisfied with the reluctant promise wrung from tho captain. They set a regular guard, of threes or fours in turn, to keep watch over the compass, and see that the ship's head was kept in the direction of the haven they looked for. The weather was baffling, and the passage was tedious The captain intended making Cork, but missed the harbour in a fog, and had got as far as Ballycotton, but, having fallen in with a Cork pilot, beat back again, so

that at length, after a passage of 14 days, the intense excitement of which may be imagined when the nature of the journey, the quality of the passengers, and the antagonistic position in which they stood to the captain and orew are considered, the ship anchored yesterday evening in the Man-of-War Roads. As fast as possible the whole band got themselves conveyed ashore to Queenstown, and testified in the most lively manner their joy at being at last assured of freedom. The enthusiasm of some rose to such a pitch that they actually kissed the soil upon which tbey first planted foot as free men. We have not learnt the ultimate intentions of this band of exiles, but it is very probable the great majority of them will go back to Italy, seeking refuge in the Sardinian kingdom. The Government of that country having, as is stated, already taken measures, in concert with the United States authorities, to have them conveyed to one of the Sardinian ports, after their arrival in New York, will now probably suit its per formance to the altered programme, and have them brought from England. Under any circumstance, Poerio will, we believe, go to Sardinia

To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis, Mr. Editor, It is an old and very common ruse among controversialists, both great and small, when utterly at a loss for arguments, to assume an air of injured feeling aud endeavor, by bringing broad accusations of personality against their adversaries, to throw dust into the eyes of the looker»-on, and thus divert their attention from the weakness of their own cause. I sincerely hope that 1 will give no additional offence, þÿ finding by owning Another þÿMember, to much in amusement, his last letter, at after so long and ominous a silence, quietly resorting to this time honored ruse, and fairly betaking himself to this convenient reluge for controversialists under difficulties. I would not, on any account , disturb him in his present quarters, for if he is satisfied with them, 1 surely havo no occasion to complain ; but I cannot help suggesting, that this asylum for the distressed, has, by age, and frequent use, been worn down þÿ to a transparency, which renders it quite in-

sufficient for his purposes. The fact is, that in these days of Newspapers, and cheap publications, men have become quite awake to such expedients, and easily see through them. Willi my reply to his first letter before them, your Readers will require no denial of this accusation of personality and violence, from me, inasmuch, as by simply comparing his communication with mine, two things will become immediately apparent þÿ lst-That my answer contains nothing half so personal or violent as the sweeping accusations brought by him, in tho first instance, and in the most indiscriminate terms, against the advocates of this cause þÿ accusations which involved in so many words, no less serious charges than these þÿ of venting wrath upon certain members of the Burgher Council for giving a conscientious vote þÿ of adopting a defiant and menacing manner þÿ of canvassing for Candidates who were pledged &c. þÿ of using language almost threatening þÿ of periling and delaying other matters of importance, for the sole purpose of carrying this measure þÿ and of professing Meekness, and Chris tian feeling, even while using violent language. And 2nd þÿ That in my reply, 1 have confined myself most strictly, to the argument, and statements advanced by your correspondent, and have never, except iu the advice kindly tendered in the last paragraph, (and which, bye the bye, we rejoice to hear, will be taken at its full value,) alluded in any way to him personally and apart from his before these two facts so plainly production. With them, I think

that it will be very difficult for him to persuade the public, that my letter is entirely a personal attack upon him, and nc argument of the case itself. I am accused of going þÿ further than exaggeþÿration þÿ and again, of being influenced by motives of self-interest in this matter. To the first accusation I simply answer þÿ 4 our þÿ ipse þÿdixit is not sufficient in such a case. Follow my example, and prove your charge, and you will find me quite ready and able to substantiate any statement that I have made To the second, 1 reply as simply ; 1 shall never þÿ trouble myself, nmlofitnlinna to protestations tn the either in public or in private, to make þÿtluvrnnt.rarv. þÿcontrary, for thoug though it is sad to think that there arc men in the world, who are so constituted, as to be incapable ol comprehending how others can possibly feel deeply by self-interest, yet the assurance on any subject without being actuated from þÿ Another þÿMember that such men do exist will not materially affect þÿ with regard to Another nty peace of mind. And þÿMember s opinion on the comparative merits of the answers which have been made to his letter of indictment, 1 can only say, that I do not at all wonder that he speaks most kindly of that, which, with a strange hallucination, he fancies, permits him to retain his old position. Under all these terrible attacks, I am, I assure you, more than comforted þÿ nay, actually buoyed up, by this significant fact, to which 1 would call the attention

of your readers þÿ namely þÿ That no attempt whatever, has been made to meet and refute a single argument, advanced by , my former letter. me in But now Mr. Editor, 1 come to the real and main object, for which 1 have solicited space in your columns again, and that object) is this To disavow most earnestly any intentional per- þÿ and sonality in þÿ to assure anything that 1 have of written Another þÿMember the entire absence of ?ny thing approaching to angry feelings on my part. Having seen that nication in your paper, and feeling his commu- he had made an ex parte statement of a cause, in which, in common with many others in the community, 1 feel a deep interest þÿ feeling also that this statement was calculated to give erroneous impressions, not only with regard to the merits of the cause þÿitself but also with regard to tho position of the great majority of those gentlemen, who support it, and are the prime movers in it I thought it right þÿ nay, a simple act of justice, alike to the cause and þÿit adherents s , to place the case in þÿit true s light. A Curious Fact in Telegraphy. þÿ It will appear an astonishing circumstauco to most of our readers that an obscure but pretty watering place on the coast of Norfolk should the other day have been holding a conversation with the metropolis via the German Ocean, Hanover, Holland, Belgium, the British Channel, and the fertile fields of Kent, yet such is nevertheless tho fact. A cable, 280 miles in length, was recently submerged from the vicinity in ot Cromer, on the Norfolk coast, to Emden Hanover, and then joined on directly to the continental system. The sauie company which laid this cable possesses two more submarine cables þÿ one from Dover to Ostend, and one from Dover to Calais þÿ likewise connected to the government telegraph abroad, and joined to London by a subterranean line running along the old mail coach road to Dover. The officials at Cromer finding Sunday, the 27th February, chat 1859, an idle day, got up some discursive through the submarine wires with the Hanoverians theso latter, perhaps disliking such þÿ their meditative habits, said, We will give you an intrusion upon þÿHolland. The officials in Holland, however, were, we presume, as deep in the enjoyment of their weeds as the Hanoverians of their profundities, and they, therefore, in like manner quietly turned off their persevering British correspondents by giving them Brussels. Here there was a rapport immediately established ; Brussels connected Cromer with its direct wires, via Ostend and Dover to London, and Cromer,

in Norfolk, was actually talking with the metropolis via an extensive ocean, three continental kingdoms, the British Channel, and the county of Kent. The signals, notwithstanding the great distance traversed, were quite perfect, and the conversation was sustained until the requirements of businezs demanded the wires for more useful, though, perhaps, not less interesting purposes.
